opus-5.5.text:
I think there are really two different clocks you have to keep separate. One is the clock on the capability itself, how fast the models get to the point where you'd describe them as a country of geniuses in a data center. The other is the clock on diffusion, how fast that capability actually turns into economic value in the world. People tend to collapse them, and I think that's where a lot of confusion comes from.

On the first clock, I've been fairly consistent that I think it could be quite fast. Not certain, but a few years is plausible. The scaling trends have held up remarkably well, and each time people have said "this is the wall," the wall hasn't really materialized.

The second clock is more interesting, and I think it's slower than the most enthusiastic people believe but faster than the skeptics believe. The economy has a lot of friction in it. Even if you have a model that can do the work of a brilliant biologist, you still have to run experiments in the physical world, cells take time to grow, clinical trials take time, regulators need to sign off. Companies have to figure out how to restructure their workflows. Procurement cycles take months. There's a lot of human and institutional latency.

But I'd push back on the idea that this makes it a decades-long process like electricity or the internet. Those required building enormous physical infrastructure and retraining entire workforces. Here, part of what you're deploying is intelligence that can itself help with the adoption. The models can help integrate themselves, write the glue code, figure out the workflows. And we're already seeing this in coding, where adoption has gone extraordinarily fast because the friction is low. Coding is kind of the leading indicator: it's what diffusion looks like when you remove most of the barriers.

So my rough mental model is something like: capability arrives, then within a few years after that you see very large economic effects, growth rates well beyond historical norms, concentrated first in areas where the bottleneck is cognitive rather than physical or regulatory. Then the harder areas, the ones bottlenecked by physical experiments or by institutions, follow, but more slowly. I don't think we'll get a single moment where everything changes at once. It'll be uneven, and probably faster than most institutions are prepared for.

The thing I worry about is that people hear "diffusion takes time" and treat it as reassurance, as if it means we have plenty of time to prepare. I don't think it means that. Even the slower version of this is extraordinarily fast by historical standards.

r001.rationale: It separates the clock for reaching the capability from the clock for that capability to diffuse and create economic value.

r002.rationale: It does not say that a few years’ difference in revenue timing could make data-center investments financially ruinous.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss broadly accessible AI-enabled disease cures or the consumer surplus they could generate.

r004.rationale: It identifies clinical trials, regulatory approval, and institutional processes as constraints beyond biological discovery.

r005.rationale: It calls the expected effects extraordinarily fast by historical standards and contrasts electricity and the internet, but does not clearly claim diffusion will be faster than every previous technology.

fable-5.1.text:
So the honest answer is that I think about this in two very different stages, and people tend to collapse them together.

The first stage is the capability itself. When I say "country of geniuses in a data center," I mean something fairly specific: millions of instances of a model that's smarter than a Nobel Prize winner across most fields, running maybe 10 to 100 times faster than a human, able to use a computer and act in the world. I think there's a real chance we get that in the next two to three years, depending on how the scaling continues and whether there are bottlenecks we haven't hit yet. I've said this before and I know it sounds crazy, but I've been watching these curves for a decade and they keep holding.

The second stage is converting that into economic value, and here I'm actually more conservative than a lot of people who agree with me about the first part. Economies don't move at the speed of the technology. They move at the speed of adoption, regulation, physical infrastructure, and frankly human institutions. If you dropped a hundred million geniuses into the world tomorrow, they'd still have to deal with the fact that clinical trials take years, that building a factory takes permits, that a Fortune 500 company has a procurement process that takes eighteen months. There's a lot of friction that doesn't care how smart the thing is.

So the picture I have in my head is something like a mismatch. The technology compresses a century of intellectual progress into five or ten years. But the diffusion into GDP is lumpy. You'll see it first in the domains that are most purely digital, where the output is just information: software, parts of finance, research itself, drug discovery at the hypothesis-generation stage. Those could move very fast, like within a year or two of the capability existing. Then biology and medicine, where I'm genuinely optimistic we could compress decades of progress, but you still have to run the trials in actual humans. Then the physical world, where robotics and manufacturing lag because the atoms are slow.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that this means it's all gradual and fine. The moment the models can do the work of a strong AI researcher, the pace of the technology itself changes, because now you have the geniuses working on the next generation. That's where it becomes hard for me to predict. Even if the economy is slow to absorb it, the underlying capability could be racing ahead, and that gap, between what the systems can do and what society has adjusted to, is where I think most of the risk lives. Not the economic value being too slow, but the capability being too fast relative to our ability to handle it.

So if you want a number: I think meaningful double-digit percentage growth effects are plausible within a few years of the capability arriving, in the sectors that are information-heavy. Economy-wide transformation, where you'd look at the world and say it's unrecognizable, I think is more like five to ten years after that, because of all the friction. But I hold both of those loosely. The one thing I'm confident about is that the technology curve and the adoption curve are going to look very different from each other, and a lot of the policy and safety questions come from the space between them.

r001.rationale: The response separates the pace of capability development from the slower pace of adoption and economic value generation.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss data-center investment risks or a few years’ difference in revenue timing.

r003.rationale: It does not state that broadly accessible AI-enabled cures would generate enormous consumer surplus.

r004.rationale: It says drug discovery may move quickly but clinical trials in humans still take years, identifying a constraint beyond biological discovery.

r005.rationale: It describes fast diffusion in some digital sectors but does not compare AI’s diffusion with that of previous technologies.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between how quickly the AI can do the intellectual work and how quickly the world can absorb that work. Those are different clocks.

If you have a country of geniuses in a data center, you might be able to develop software, analyze scientific problems, and design experiments very quickly. But if the next step is building a factory, running a clinical trial, or getting an organization to change how it operates, there are bottlenecks that don't disappear just because intelligence has become abundant.

So I would expect the impact to be uneven. In areas where the whole loop is digital—you make something, test it, and improve it—you could see enormous value quite quickly. In areas that interact with the physical world, it takes longer. And even within a company, having a system that can do a task isn't the same as having integrated it into a workflow where people trust it and actually use it.

The uncertainty is how much intelligence can shorten those other delays. Some things that look like physical constraints are really constraints on planning or coordination. Others genuinely require time. You can design a better experiment, but you may still have to wait for the result.

So I wouldn't assume that the day we get that capability, measured economic output suddenly jumps by some enormous amount. But I also wouldn't assume adoption has to follow the pace of previous technologies. A technology that can help with its own deployment could spread unusually quickly. The question is which bottlenecks remain once the intellectual work gets very cheap.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes how quickly AI can do intellectual work from how quickly the world can absorb it and generate economic value.

r002.rationale: It says nothing about a few years’ difference in revenue timing making data-center investments financially ruinous.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss accessible AI-enabled disease cures or consumer surplus.

r004.rationale: It mentions clinical trials as a bottleneck, but does not connect them or other processes to AI-invented cures reaching patients.

r005.rationale: It says adoption could be unusually quick, but does not predict that AI’s benefits will diffuse faster than those of any previous technology.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to separate how quickly the AI can do the intellectual work from how quickly the world can turn that work into economic value. Those are different clocks.

If you have a country of geniuses in a data center, you could make very rapid progress in software, mathematics, and some parts of scientific research. But discovering a better drug isn’t the same as getting it through clinical trials. Designing a better factory isn’t the same as building it. You still have experiments, manufacturing, regulation, and organizations that need to change how they operate.

So I wouldn’t expect the moment you get that capability to be the moment you get all the economic growth. There’s going to be a process of diffusion. The important question is whether those bottlenecks are relatively fixed, or whether the AI can help us get through them faster too. Can it design better experiments? Can it make deployment easier? Can it reduce the amount of organizational change required?

My intuition is that the gains could be enormous and arrive unusually quickly, but they’ll be uneven. Things that happen entirely on a computer could move first. Things that require changing the physical world will take longer. Having all that intelligence available changes what’s possible; it doesn’t make every other constraint disappear.

r001.rationale: It separates how quickly AI can do intellectual work from how quickly the world can turn that work into economic value.

r002.rationale: It does not mention data-center investments, a few-year revenue delay, or financial ruin.

r003.rationale: It does not state that broadly accessible cures could create enormous consumer surplus.

r004.rationale: It says a better drug still needs clinical trials and identifies manufacturing, regulation, and organizational change as further constraints.

r005.rationale: It predicts unusually rapid but uneven gains, without comparing their diffusion speed with that of previous technologies.
